extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and distinctions for what counts as legitimate induction (inference from observed cases to general propositions) and for distinguishing genuine induction from related or spurious procedures (mathematical demonstration, mere enumeration, tests of inconceivability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the operation of discovering and proving general propositions: inferring that what is known to be true in particular cases will be true in all cases which resemble them in certain assignable respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that the same principles apply when indirectly ascertaining individual facts (an individual fact can be established by induction just as a general truth can). Generals are collections of particulars definite in kind but indefinite in number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of inductive principles for general and individual inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles and rules of inference are the same whether we infer general propositions or individual facts; a complete logic of the sciences is a complete logic of all legitimate induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by astronomy: determining the moon's distance used a chain of inductions ultimately yielding a general theorem; whether the conclusion is 'a fact' or 'a general proposition' the logical conditions are the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of an induction depends on the number and nature of instances, not mere exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate generalization depends on the sufficiency of the instances observed—their number and character—not on having examined every member of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: concluding 'all animals have a nervous system' can be an induction that legitimately predicts yet-undiscovered species will have nervous systems if the observed instances are of the right kind and number; conversely, merely asserting 'all known animals' is not the same as a true induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper 'induction' as mere summation of known cases (not genuine inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: An operation which merely re-states a collection of known particular propositions (e.g., asserting a generality that covers only the enumerated individuals) is not true induction because it involves no inference from known to unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'perfect induction' in some logic books when the premise enumerates every individual—this is useful as notation but not part of the investigation of truth. Examples: 'All the planets shine by the sun's light' asserted only because each known planet does so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstrations and diagrammatic proofs are not induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many processes in mathematics that yield general propositions are not inductive because they do not infer from particular observed instances but derive the general truth by demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A diagram-based proof shows a property in a particular figure but, because the demonstrative reasoning applies generally, we express it as a universal theorem. This is 'induction by parity of reasoning' (not proper induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical extrapolation of sequences requires a priori justification
rubrics_metrics.description: When mathematicians extend an algebraic or arithmetical series after computing many terms, they do so only when a priori considerations show the same generative rule applies to subsequent terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filling in future terms without such justification would be a bad induction; the apparent inference rests on demonstrable mode-of-formation rather than mere count of past terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-limit for inconceivability test (Spencer's Universal Postulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test that 'an abortive effort to conceive the negation of a proposition shows that the cognition is one of which the predicate invariably exists along with its subject' is only legitimately applicable to simple propositions assented to on immediate inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex propositions, whose subject and predicate are indirectly related through many simpler propositions, cannot be properly tested by immediate inconceivability (example: the Pythagorean theorem requires mediate proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to conceive the negative does not prove objective inseparability
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure to separate two ideas in thought (inconceivability of the negation) proves only inseparability in the present mind, not a corresponding inseparability in fact or in other minds or future states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after understanding Copernican proof we nevertheless can more easily conceive sunrise as the sun moving; inability to conceive otherwise does not make the earth's motion untrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is the preferable ground for testing propositions rather than inconceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: When universal and elementary propositions are represented in early, unvarying experience, the inconceivability of their negation is accounted for by experience; but we should test truth by appealing to experience itself rather than to a test of familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that appealing to inconceivability may disguise insufficiency of experience; it's enough to know one has seen the fact repeatedly and others with opportunity declare the same, rather than attempting to recall every instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Contradiction is grounded in observed exclusiveness of mental/phenomenal states
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that the same proposition cannot at the same time be true and false (Principium Contradictionis) is not merely verbal but a generalization from experience: belief and disbelief are distinct and exclusive mental states, paralleled by contrary phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill accepts it as one of our familiar generalizations from experience rather than a purely verbal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Excluded Middle has limits—predicates must be intelligibly predicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that any proposition must be either true or false holds only when the predicate is one which can in any intelligible sense be attributed to the subject; otherwise a third state, 'unmeaning,' is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples: sentences whose predicate is inapplicable (e.g., 'Abracadabra is a second intention') are neither true nor false; extension of Excluded Middle to noumena (things-in-themselves) is unwarranted because predicability may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor: invention (selection of inductions) vs. validation (tests of validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical inquiry the chief difficulty is selecting which inductions to employ (an inventive task of sagacity and knowledge); once a candidate induction is proposed, science supplies principles and tests to judge its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an advocate's skill lies in bringing a case under appropriate general propositions; the rules of logic then determine whether the facts fall within those propositions and whether the inductions themselves are legitimate.
